declarations.description:
Conway's life across the whole visible region. Drawing seeds cells; dead
cells leave a fading trail. Cells beyond the region's edge count as dead, so
a colony meets the edge and dies there rather than wrapping round.

It draws white on transparent, fading by alpha, into its own image data put
whole each frame, though only the box where cells changed is repainted.

declarations.description:
A small critter on the bottom edge of the viewport. It naps curled up, wakes
to a tap, follows the pointer, delights in being rubbed, and walks to any
crumb a tap tosses. Left alone it dozes off again, and the sleeper stops
asking for frames once its last z has floated away.

It is simulated in fixed 60 Hz steps, so its pace does not depend on the
display, and drawn white by alpha into its own image data.

A bed of pins. Pointer movement and presses push pins down; each springs
back at its own rate once left alone. A press held longer goes deeper.

its own image data put whole each frame.

is flat, waking by timer for the next raindrop while the rain lasts.

declarations.description:
Falling sand in a tray the size of the visible screen. Grains pile on its
bottom edge and slip down dunes; the sieve floor drips grains through, so an
untouched tab slowly empties and the loop can stop. A double-tap tips the
tray out: gravity reverses and the new floor is wide open until the sand is
gone.

Until the first input a small settled dune rests on the floor as a hint that
the tray is live. It is frozen and costs nothing; the first input hands it
to the normal sim, so it drains like any poured sand.

declarations.name: cellScale
declarations.description:
How many canvas pixels span one design cell of `designCellPx` pixels, with
the canvas `width` pixels drawn across the reference viewport. Multiply a

declarations.name: fixedStep
declarations.description:
Paces a toy's simulation in whole steps of `stepMs` however often frames
arrive, so a 120 Hz display does not run it twice as fast. A pause longer
than `maxCatchUpMs`, like a hidden tab, is not replayed. The first frame
after `restart`, which a toy calls whenever its loop stops, runs one step
instead of replaying the idle gap.

declarations.name: frameLoop
declarations.description:
The animation loop the toys here run on, so each need not write its own.
`step` runs on an animation frame with its time, and the loop asks for the
next frame only while `step` returns true, so it sleeps once nothing moves.
`wake` asks for a frame unless one is pending. `stop` cancels a pending
frame, as `cancelAnimationFrame` does, and a later `wake` starts the loop
again; inside a step none is pending, so the step's return still decides.

A toy paced by `fixedStep` restarts it, and a toy that sleeps on a timer
sets it, where its step returns false.

measures it on start and on `resize`. A canvas not laid out yet counts as
visible whole.

declarations.description:
A lava lamp: blobs warm near the bottom, rise, cool near the top and sink.
Press a blob to hold and drag it, let go to fling it; tapping empty glass
shoves the wax away and hovering nudges it. Left alone the lamp cools to a
stop, so an untouched tab costs nothing, and any input warms it again.

It draws white, each band of wax a different alpha, so an owner can recolour
it without losing the bands.

declarations.name: renderBlobs
declarations.description:
Bands the summed influence of the blobs over the visible cells. A blob's
`r² / (d² + 0.5)` falls off slowly, so it is split at `TAIL`: the part above
it is added exactly within the box where it exists, and the capped remainder,
which is smooth, is sampled on a coarse lattice and interpolated. The cost
follows the blobs' size, not their count times the whole grid.

`<pixel-backdrop>` fills the viewport with a live `<emulated-canvas>`, its
child, and runs a backdrop toy on it. The toy only draws on the canvas and
listens to it, as it would on any canvas; the element picks the toy, styles
the canvas (the display's palette, the drifting noise, the dissolve between
toys), and passes it the pointer. The layer is fixed and non-interactive,
so the page above it paints its own solid panels over the result. Its
layout is `pixel-backdrop.css`, which also holds the knobs' defaults; a
page overrides them on its own `:root`.

The element owns its render knobs, which `configure()` can tweak live.
`resolveLook` turns them, the toy's look and the display into the
`<emulated-canvas>`'s `data-*` attributes, its public API, and the
properties the backdrop's stylesheet reads. Under reduced motion it runs
no toy.

A canvas stand-in that hides its display surface. Consumers draw into an
`OffscreenCanvas` through `getContext`, and a real `<canvas>` in a closed
shadow root is blitted from that bitmap.

`data-width` and `data-height` size the inner (logical) canvas. The outer
canvas can magnify each logical pixel into a cell: `data-scale` sets the
cell size in CSS pixels (default 1), `data-gap` the space between cells
(default 0), and `data-shape` the cell form, inscribed in the cell:
`"square"` (default), `"circle"`, `"ring"`, `"diamond"`, `"hex"` (pointy
top, odd rows half a cell right), `"triangle"` (two cells wide, up and down
by turns, interlocking), `"dash"` (a horizontal capsule),
`"slash"` (bottom left to top right) or `"cross"`. With the defaults the
outer canvas is a straight 1:1 mirror. A page can instead size cells from
CSS by setting `--emulated-canvas-scale` to a length on the element, which
then follows viewport changes without any script.

Gaps and the rest of each cell outside its shape are painted over the
cells rather than cut out, in `--emulated-canvas-gap-color` (default
`Canvas`, the page's default background); set it to whatever shows behind
the element. A pixel shadow is cast from square cells whatever the shape.

`data-shadow` (0–100, default 0) casts each pixel's shadow, like an LCD's
segments over their backplate: each pixel darkens what lies under it by how
much darker it is than unlit, at that opacity, offset by `data-shadow-x` and
`data-shadow-y` (whole CSS pixels, default 0). With a palette unlit is its
base, so only pixels darker than the base cast a shadow; without one it is
white. The shadow is cast from the frame's pixels on each present, so a
shadow over drawing other than a whole-bitmap `putImageData`, with no pass
on, reads the bitmap back.

Effects are `SHADERS`, an ordered list of per-pixel passes (a drifting
noise, a two-colour palette and an LCD's ghosting), each documenting its own
live `data-*` knobs in `shaders/`. They run on the logical bitmap, never at
display resolution, so each costs the same however large the cells are
drawn.

The canvas presents on its own, the way a plain `<canvas>` shows what is
drawn on it: drawing through the 2D context queues a present for when the
drawing code returns, so a frame drawn in an animation frame shows in that
same frame, and several calls cost one present. While a pass is still
changing the display, the canvas keeps presenting every animation frame, or
at about 8 fps for a pass that only drifts, then stops. `data-manual` opts
out: the owner calls `present()` itself.

The context is the inner canvas's own, with only its pixel-writing methods
wrapped to note that the bitmap changed: nothing is proxied or replayed, so
drawing costs what it costs on any canvas. A `putImageData` of the whole
bitmap hands the passes those pixels, sparing them a read-back; any other
drawing is read back once, on the present after it.

declarations.summary: A canvas stand-in that draws its bitmap as magnified cells through per-pixel passes.

declarations.name: MAX_GHOST
declarations.description: Retention is capped below 1 so the panel can never freeze on one frame.

One element's passes, built from its shaders and configured from its
`dataset`. A present asks `active` first, so that with no pass on it can
skip reading the pixels back, then hands them to `apply`.
declarations.name: Pipeline

members.name: active
members.description:
Whether any pass is on. A pass found off after being on is rebuilt here,
so when it comes back it starts from the current frame, not a stale one.

members.name: apply
members.description:
Runs every active pass over `pixels`, in order, and returns how soon to
present next. Call `active` first each frame, as it rebuilds the passes
that went off; it is separate so a caller can skip reading pixels back.

declarations.name: SHAPES
declarations.description: Every cell form, the default first.

Puts a bitmap-sized frame on screen: a real `<canvas>` (the display) in the
given shadow root, the stylesheet that draws its pixels as cells, and the
echo that casts their shadow.
declarations.name: Presenter

members.name: needsPixels
members.description: A shadow and a shifted canvas are drawn from the frame's pixels, so while one is on, `show` must be given them.

members.name: configure
members.description: Rewrites the stylesheet, so it belongs to attribute changes, never to a present.

members.name: show
members.description: Shows the frame: image data as its pixels, a bitmap as drawn. False when the display cannot draw.

declarations.name: mulberry32
declarations.description: A tiny deterministic PRNG, so the noise field is stable across reloads.

declarations.name: NOISE_OFFSET_X
declarations.description:
Simplex is exactly zero on integer lattice points, so sample off-lattice:
without this a 1-pixel feature size would flatten to a constant.

declarations.name: makeNoise2D
declarations.description: Build a seeded 2D simplex field, returning values in [-1, 1].

declarations.name: makeCoarseNoise
declarations.description:
A noise layer over a `columns` × `rows` field that samples `noise` only every
`step` cells along each axis and fills between bilinearly. Smooth noise
barely bends over a few cells, so this costs about 1/step² of sampling every
cell for a near-identical layer. Each call raises every cell to `amount`
times the noise mapped to 0–1, where that is brighter; cell (x, y) samples
the noise at `(x * frequency + offsetX, y * frequency + offsetY)`.

declarations.name: texture
declarations.description: The backdrop's mottle: broad blotches with a finer grain over them.

declarations.name: landscape
declarations.description:
A seeded skyline over mottled ground that darkens with depth, in 0–1 cell
values. Its sizes were tuned in cells of an 80-column grid; `scale` is how
many cells of this grid span one of those.

declarations.name: crags
declarations.description:
A jagged range lit from the upper left, in 0.3–1 cell values that grow with
shadow, after the browserbase.com hero. Each cell is jittered, so a palette
of few levels stipples between them as the hero's does. Sized like
`landscape`.

declarations.name: multiplyOverlay
declarations.description:
Writes into `colour` the paint, and returns the alpha, that composited over
`base` as ordinary paint gives what multiplying it by `factor` (0–1 per
channel) gives, so a layer can darken without a blend mode. Paint has one
alpha for all three channels, so over any other colour a channel is off by
`(factor − min factor)·(base − colour under)`: exact in the channel darkened
most. `colour` is the caller's, so painting per pixel allocates nothing.

declarations.name: hexRgb
declarations.description: `#rgb` or `#rrggbb` as `[r, g, b]`, or undefined for any other form.

declarations.default: { attributes: ["data-ghost", "data-ghost-rise", "data-ghost-fall"], create() { let panel: Float32Array | undefined; let riseTau = 0; let fallTau = 0; let active = false; return { configure(data) { const rise = retention(data.ghostRise ?? data.ghost); const fall = retention(data.ghostFall ?? data.ghost); riseTau = timeConstant(rise); fallTau = timeConstant(fall); active = rise > 0 || fall > 0; }, active: () => active, apply(pixels, { elapsedMs }) { if (panel?.length !== pixels.length) { // Seed the panel with this frame so it starts opaque; otherwise a high // retention would fade in from transparent. panel = Float32Array.from(pixels); return "still"; } const rise = response(riseTau, elapsedMs); const fall = response(fallTau, elapsedMs); let changing = false; for (let pixel = 0; pixel < pixels.length; pixel += 4) { const brightening = pixels[pixel] + pixels[pixel + 1] + pixels[pixel + 2] > panel[pixel] + panel[pixel + 1] + panel[pixel + 2]; const share = brightening ? rise : fall; for (let i = pixel; i < pixel + 4; i += 1) { const target = pixels[i]; const level = panel[i] + (target - panel[i]) * share; if (Math.abs(target - level) < SETTLED_LEVELS) { panel[i] = target; } else { panel[i] = level; pixels[i] = level; changing = true; } } } return changing ? declarations.description:
Emulates an LCD's slow pixel response: every channel moves toward the new
frame along an exponential with time constant τ, so fast motion leaves a
fading trail. Driving it by elapsed time rather than per frame keeps the
trail the same length at any refresh rate, and keeping the state in floats
lets it land on the frame exactly instead of stalling a few 8-bit steps
short.

Real panels brighten and darken at different speeds, so a pixel getting
brighter overall follows the rise curve in every channel and one getting
darker the fall curve. Choosing per pixel rather than per channel keeps a
colour change from splitting into a fast and a slow channel.

`data-ghost` (0–100, default 0) is the percentage of the previous frame the
panel keeps per 60 Hz frame, capped just below 100 so the panel can never
freeze. `data-ghost-rise` and `data-ghost-fall` (same range, each defaulting
to `data-ghost`) set it apart for pixels getting brighter and darker.

declarations.name: SHADERS
declarations.description:
Per-pixel passes over the logical bitmap, in order. To add an effect, write a
`Shader` and add it to this list.

declarations.name: MAX_NOISE_STEP
declarations.description:
The noise is sampled at most this many pixels apart and filled in between.
At the backdrop's feature size that is a quarter of the samples per axis,
within 0.02 RMS (0.075 at worst) of sampling every pixel.

"idle" : "still"; }, }; }, }
declarations.description:
A drifting simplex field under the frame, so its dark pixels shimmer: each
channel is lifted to the noise where that is brighter, like a `lighten`
blend, and the drawing shows on top. `data-noise` is its intensity (0–100),
`data-noise-scale` its feature size in pixels (default 8) and
`data-noise-speed` how fast it drifts (0–100, default 0). At the speeds the
backdrop uses the drift moves about a pixel per 60 Hz frame on a desktop
screen, so it redraws at the idle rate.

declarations.description:
Recolours the frame: each pixel's luma, over black, picks its place on the
scale from `data-palette-base` (dark) to `data-palette-ink` (light), CSS
colours that are both set or the pass is off, so a consumer can draw in any
colour and still show in the palette. `data-palette-stops`, colours
separated by spaces, spaces more colours evenly between them, so the scale
runs through each.
`data-palette-levels` (2 or more) snaps each pixel to the nearest of that
many evenly spaced shades, like a panel with few grey levels; as many as the
colours lands each shade on one. `data-palette-dither`, with levels, mixes
the two shades either side of a pixel's luma in a 4 x 4 ordered pattern in
proportion, so detail fainter than a step still shows, as a panel shows grey
on its few levels. The pattern is fixed to the bitmap, so moving shapes do
not shimmer. The scale is a 256-entry table, rebuilt only when a knob
changes.
